name: Bardeen Regular Black Hole
description: A black hole with horizons and no singularity, which James Bardeen proposed in 1968. A ball of de Sitter space sits where Schwarzschild's singularity would be, and Eloy Ayón-Beato and Alberto García showed in 2000 that the field of a magnetic monopole in a nonlinear electrodynamics is its source.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and the length $g$ is the charge of the magnetic monopole. We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Can a black hole keep its horizon and lose its singularity? A trapped surface forces a singularity on any spacetime with a noncompact Cauchy surface and matter of nonnegative energy density: that is Roger Penrose's theorem of 1965 [penrose1965]. Three years later, at the conference GR5 in Tiflis, James Bardeen showed one that does [borde1997, ayonbeato2000]. He took the Reissner-Nordström metric for inspiration and replaced its function $1 - r_s/r + r_q^2/r^2$ by $$f(r) = 1 - \frac{r_s r^2}{\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2}},$$ with $r_s$ the Schwarzschild radius and $g$ a second length [borde1994, borde1997]. The trapped surfaces stay, between two horizons, and the singularity goes [borde1994]. The proceedings were published in the Soviet Union, and Arvind Borde remarked in 1997 that the paper "is not readily available" [borde1997].¶The model is Schwarzschild's far away and de Sitter's at the centre: $f$ approaches $1 - r_s/r$ at large $r$, and $f \approx 1 - r_sr^2/g^3$ near $r = 0$ [ansoldi2008]. The curvature invariants are finite everywhere, the centre included [ayonbeato2000]. A small enough $g$ leaves the black hole two horizons: for $g < 2r_s/3\sqrt{3}$ the function $f$ vanishes at two radii, an event horizon and an inner horizon [ayonbeato2000]. At $g = 2r_s/3\sqrt{3}$ the two merge into one extreme horizon, and for larger $g$ there is no horizon [ayonbeato2000]. Read through Einstein's equations, the metric has a source that obeys the weak energy condition [borde1997, ayonbeato2000]. It breaks the strong energy condition near the centre, and a regular spherical black hole must break it in every static region under its event horizon, a theorem of Oleg Zaslavskii's from 2010 [zaslavskii2010].¶Stephen Hawking and George Ellis took the model as a counterexample: a trapped surface does not imply a singularity unless one assumes either a global Cauchy surface or the strong energy condition [hawking1973, borde1997, ayonbeato2000]. Bardeen himself noted that space changes its topology inside the hole: a slice outside is $S^2 \times \mathbb{R}$, and a slice between the two centres $r = 0$ is a 3-sphere [borde1994, borde1997]. There light rays can "wrap around the universe", and the two families of rays from a trapped surface come to a focus at two antipodal centres, with no singularity [borde1994, borde1997]. In a large class of spacetimes that obey the weak energy condition, Borde proved in 1997, a regular black hole requires this change of topology from open to closed [borde1997]. He gave the whole family the name "Bardeen black holes" [borde1997].¶The de Sitter core goes back to 1966, when Andrei Sakharov proposed that matter at very high density has the equation of state $p = -\rho$, that of a cosmological constant [sakharov1966, ansoldi2008]. That year Erast Gliner took a spacetime filled with such a vacuum to be the final stage of gravitational collapse, where the singularity would be [gliner1966, ansoldi2008]. Bardeen's metric was the first black hole to realise the idea [ansoldi2008]. A thin layer can join part of the inside of a Schwarzschild black hole to de Sitter space, the model of Valeri Frolov, Moissei Markov, and Viatcheslav Mukhanov from 1989 [frolov1989, frolov1990closed, borde1997]. An exponential makes the same passage smoothly: with $f = 1 - (r_s/r)\left(1 - e^{-r^3/r_*^3}\right)$, Irina Dymnikova's black hole of 1992 is Schwarzschild's far away and de Sitter's at the centre [dymnikova1992, ansoldi2008]. A regular black hole can be exactly Schwarzschild's outside its horizon and still obey the weak energy condition: Marc Mars, M. Mercè Martín-Prats, and José Senovilla built one in 1996 [mars1996, borde1997].¶The source of a regular black hole can be a field: in Eloy Ayón-Beato and Alberto García's solution of 1998 it is the electric field of a nonlinear electrodynamics, Maxwell's theory in weak fields [ayonbeato1998]. Bardeen's own metric got its source from them in 2000: $g$ is the charge of a magnetic monopole, whose field obeys a nonlinear electrodynamics with the Lagrangian $$L(F) = \frac{3}{2sg^2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2g^2F}}{1 + \sqrt{2g^2F}}\right)^{5/2},$$ where $F = F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}/4$ and $s = g/r_s$, in units with $G = c = 1$ [ayonbeato2000]. In weak fields this theory is stronger than Maxwell's, $L \sim F^{5/4}$ [ayonbeato2000]. The charge has to be magnetic: no one Lagrangian $L(F)$ with the Maxwell limit admits a regular centre with an electric charge, Kirill Bronnikov proved in 2001, and the electric models need different Lagrangians at different radii [bronnikov2001]. Ayón-Beato and García carried the metric through both horizons in advanced and retarded Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates, and found the global structure of Reissner-Nordström with the singularity smoothed into the origin of the spherical coordinates [ayonbeato2000].¶A regular black hole can also form and evaporate: Sean Hayward let the mass of a similar metric depend on the advanced time in 2006, as Vaidya's does, and no singularity appears at any stage [hayward2006]. Regular black holes had been dismissed as unphysical for their Cauchy horizon, and Hayward replied that in a hole that evaporates the Cauchy horizon "is no more real than the event horizon" [hayward2006]. Bardeen returned to the idea in 2014 with an evaporating black hole whose singularity is "replaced by an initially small non-singular core inside an inner apparent horizon" [bardeen2014]. The inner horizon is unstable to the mass inflation of Eric Poisson and Werner Israel, on the timescale $1/\kappa_-$ of its surface gravity, by the 2018 calculation of Raúl Carballo-Rubio, Francesco Di Filippo, Stefano Liberati, Costantino Pacilio, and Matt Visser [carballorubio2018, poisson1990]. The evaporation, they found, takes an infinite time [carballorubio2018].

related.text: Bardeen took this charged black hole for inspiration. The two share a tower of exteriors and interiors, and Bardeen's has a regular centre where Reissner-Nordström's has a timelike singularity [borde1994, ayonbeato2000].
Bardeen's black hole with the monopole switched off. At $g = 0$ the metric function is Schwarzschild's $1 - r_s/r$, and the singularity is back.

The core of Bardeen's black hole. Near the centre $f \approx 1 - r_sr^2/g^3$, de Sitter's static metric with $\Lambda = 3r_s/g^3$, and in the limit $g \to \infty$ at fixed $r_s/g^3$ the whole metric is de Sitter's [ansoldi2008].
Another black hole with no singularity. Where Bardeen's has a regular centre, Simpson and Visser's has a throat of radius $a$, and its inside bounces into another universe [simpson2019].
A regular black hole of the same kind whose metric function is a ratio of polynomials. Sean Hayward let its mass change in time in 2006, so that it forms and evaporates [hayward2006].
Gliner's vacuum with $p = -\rho$ as the whole interior of a collapsed star, held under a thin shell with no horizon [mazur2004, gliner1966].

Ori's model of a charged hole with radiation crossing it, whose mass function grows without limit at the inner horizon. Carried over to Bardeen's metric it gives an exponentially growing mass at the inner horizon as well [carballorubio2021].

A point charge of Born and Infeld's nonlinear electrodynamics, to which Hoffmann gave its gravity in 1935. Its charge is electric and its centre a conical point or a singularity, where Bardeen's monopole has a regular centre [hoffmann1935, gibbonsrasheed1995].

coordinates.name: Static Spherical

parameters.description: Charge of the magnetic monopole, a length. The black hole has two horizons for $g < 2r_s/3\sqrt{3}$, with $r_\pm$ their radii and $\kappa_\pm$ their surface gravities, one for $g = 2r_s/3\sqrt{3}$, and none beyond

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{r_s\,r\left(r^2 - 2g^2\right)\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)}{2\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^4}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{r_s\,r\left(r^2 - 2g^2\right)}{2\left(r^2 + g^2\right)\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)}\dot{r}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)}{\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2}}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2}}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the retarded time $u = ct - r_*$ a length, where $dr_*/dr = \left(1 - r_s r^2/\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2}\right)^{-1}$ and $r_* = 0$ at $r = 0$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{r_s\,r\left(r^2 - 2g^2\right)\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)}{2\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^4}\dot{u}^2 + \dfrac{r_s\,r\left(r^2 - 2g^2\right)}{\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{5/2}}\dot{u}\dot{r} - \dfrac{r\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)}{\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2}}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{r\left(\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2} - r_s\,r^2\right)\sin^2\theta}{\left(r^2 + g^2\right)^{3/2}}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
